Thanks for reminding me. I havent seen any follow ups on this particular collapse. As odd as the cooking oil cans might look, they aren't necessarily the reason the building collapsed. While the building itself is supposed to be reinforced concrete, depending on how the structural system was designed, the building could have been insufficient, or since it had been through a previous sesimic event, damaged.

Now as for the cooking oil cans in the walls, masonry design allows for the use of nonstructural materials to be used as facing for actual structural wythes or for interior nonstructural partition walls. Some of those materials include ceramic tile, tera cotta, and glass, so a more esoteric material as a nonstructural facing isnt inconcieveable, though a cursory glance at ther photos makes me think that the entire structure was built as shear walls with these oil cans being grouted into the walls and their thickness "claimed" as an actual wall design value, but I would need to see more info on the original documents before I could lable that as the main cause.

The fact that the building toppled while uprooting its foundation is something else to consider. See most buildings thst fail under dynamic loading like seismic, dont uproot themselves. Most experience sidesway behavior and tend to fail at a discontinuity in the structural system, things like soft storey elevations where one floor is taller than the ones above it, or oddly shaped layouts. Even then the collapses tend to be partial due to lateral buckling or walls or columns, like you see in all the other buildings that collapses on that page, despite the high deflections in upper storeys. Being uprooted makes me think the connection to the foundation was damaged previously or not sufficient. When you see this kind of behavior in structural failures, it is usually a geotechnical/foundation design issue at heart.
